name: Zoroastrianism
era: From Zarathustra, before 600 BCE, to today
line: Choose the truth in thought, in word and in deed, and make the world better for it.

quote.text: Listen with your ears to the best things. Reflect with a clear mind, each person for themselves, upon the two choices.
quote.source: Gathas, Yasna 30.2, after the translation of Stanley Insler, 1975

quotes.text: Righteousness is the best good. It is happiness. Happiness comes to the one who is righteous for the sake of the best righteousness.
quotes.source: The first prayer a Zoroastrian child learns; a common English rendering

quotes.text: Happiness comes to the one who brings happiness to others.
quotes.source: Gathas, Yasna 43.1, in its common English paraphrase

quotes.text: I pledge myself to the well-thought thought, the well-spoken word and the well-done deed.
quotes.source: Yasna 12.8, in a common English rendering

quotes.text: What is right, that is my desire. To the man who is a follower of the Lie I am not a friend.
quotes.source: Inscription DNb on his tomb at Naqsh-e Rustam, trans. Roland G. Kent, 1950

words.usage: The one uncreated God, wholly good, creator of all that is good. Ohrmazd in Middle Persian.
The way things ought to be and at their best are: the order of the stars, the honesty of a contract, the health of a field.
Falsehood, disorder and decay. The opposite of asha in the world and in the mind.

words.meaning: Good thoughts, good words, good deeds
words.usage: The whole ethic in three words. The order matters: deed follows word, and word follows thought.
The creative, life-giving spirit through which Ahura Mazda acts.
The destructive spirit, source of death and falsehood. Ahriman in Middle Persian. He is not God’s equal and will be defeated.
Six or seven divine qualities of Ahura Mazda, each guarding a part of creation: good mind, truth, good rule, devotion, wholeness and immortality.
Clear, kindly thought. The first of the immortals and guardian of cattle and all animals.
Serene, loving attention. Guardian of the earth.
Power used well. The dominion a person has over their own choices, and the just order to come.
The visible sign of asha: light, warmth and energy. Zoroastrians pray before fire. They do not worship it.
The highest grade of consecrated fire, made from sixteen sources including lightning. There are nine in the world.
The Parsi word. In Iran it is an atashkadeh or dar-e mehr, the door of Mithra.
What survives of a much larger body of sacred texts, in an ancient Iranian language.
Seventeen songs in very old, difficult verse, the only words that come from the prophet himself.
A plain white cotton undershirt with a tiny pocket at the throat to be filled with good deeds.
A cord of seventy-two lambswool threads wound three times round the waist and untied and retied with prayers several times a day.
The ceremony at which a child first puts on the sudreh and kusti. Sedreh pushi in Iran.
The priesthood is hereditary. A high priest is a dastur.
The long daily rite performed by priests before the fire, and the text recited in it, which contains the Gathas.
The final renewal of the world, when evil is overcome and creation is restored to perfection. People help to bring it about.

words.meaning: The one who will bring benefit
words.usage: The future saviour who will lead the last renewal. In the Gathas the word may mean anyone who works for good.
The bridge each soul crosses after death. It is wide for the truthful and a razor’s edge for the false.
One’s inner self. At the bridge it meets the soul as a beautiful or a hideous figure and says: I am your own deeds.
The higher part of each person, which exists before birth and protects the living.
A man rising from a winged disc, carved at Persepolis. Now the best known emblem of the faith.
The new year at the spring equinox, the greatest festival, celebrated across the Iranian world by people of every religion.
One of six festivals of the farming year, kept with communal meals to which rich and poor contribute and sit together.
A greeting and a blessing. The joy that comes of living by asha.
A ritual handclasp and greeting exchanged after prayers: may we be united in righteousness.

practices.name: Three knots
practices.instructions: After washing, stand facing a source of light: the sun, a window, a lamp. Take a belt, a cord or the hem of your shirt in both hands. Tie one knot, or touch it, and say: today, good thoughts. A second: good words. A third: good deeds. Then say in your own words that you choose the side of truth today and reject the lie. Stand still for a few breaths in the light.
practices.why: Zoroastrians untie and retie the kusti, the sacred cord, on rising and through the day, facing the light and renewing their commitment. This is a guest’s version of the same resolve, without the cord itself.
variations: Say the three words again each time you wash your hands.
Learn the Ashem Vohu in English and say it once.

practices.name: Keep a flame
practices.instructions: Light a candle or an oil lamp in a clean, safe place. Sit before it for ten minutes. Look at the flame steadily. Think of what it does: it gives light, it gives warmth, it rises, it cannot be made dirty. Ask what in you is like that and what dims it. Put it out by pinching or covering the wick. Do not blow on it.
practices.why: Fire is the sign of asha and of the divine presence. In the great temples a fire has been fed by hand five times a day for centuries. A priest covers his mouth so that his breath does not touch it.
variations: Sit facing the rising or setting sun instead.
Keep one lamp burning through an evening and tend it.
Add a little sandalwood or incense, as worshippers do.

practices.name: The true word
practices.instructions: Choose one moment today when a lie, a flattering half-truth or a convenient silence would be easier, and tell the truth instead, plainly and without unkindness. Keep every promise you make today, including the small ones about time. In the evening count the day’s untruths, including the ones told to yourself.
practices.why: The religion’s deepest opposition is between truth and the lie. The Persians, wrote Herodotus, taught their sons three things: to ride, to draw the bow and to speak the truth.
variations: Correct one false impression you have allowed to stand.
Pay a bill or a debt on the day it is due.
Say I do not know when you do not.

practices.name: Tend the creation
practices.instructions: Do one thing that leaves the physical world in better order: clear rubbish from a stream or a street, water a tree, plant something, clean a neglected corner, feed an animal, mend what is broken. Take care not to foul water, soil or fire while you do it. Think of it as taking a side.
practices.why: Each of the seven creations has a divine guardian: sky, water, earth, plants, animals, humankind and fire. Humans are the stewards. Zoroastrianism has been called the first ecological religion for this reason.
variations: Never pour anything dirty into a river or the sea.
Plant something that will outlive the Onda.
Care for a dog, which the tradition holds in special honour.

practices.name: The evening account
practices.instructions: Sit quietly and go through the day in three columns: thoughts, words, deeds. In each, name one that was good and one that was not. For the bad ones, decide on a concrete repair for tomorrow and resolve on it. Then do something that gives joy before bed: music, a story, laughter with someone. Gloom is counted a fault.
practices.why: After death the soul’s thoughts, words and deeds are weighed, and its own conscience meets it at the bridge. Reviewing them each night is the obvious preparation. The tradition also insists on cheerfulness and forbids despair.
variations: Write the three columns in a notebook.
End by giving something to a cause that helps strangers.
Share the review with a friend.

tasks.name: Give to a cause that will outlast you
tasks.meta: Parsi philanthropy built hospitals, schools and wells

tasks.name: Set a table of seven good things
tasks.meta: The haft-sin idea: growth, health, sweetness, patience

tasks.name: Read Yasna 30, the hymn of the two spirits
Listen to the Ashem Vohu chanted in Avestan
tasks.meta: Listen · one minute, three thousand years old

tasks.name: Look at the winged figure above the doors of Persepolis
Play backgammon
tasks.meta: Games · the Persian game of fate and choice

tasks.name: Journal: one good thought, one good word, one good deed
The two choices: where did you choose today?
Plant something or water a tree
Light a candle at dusk and keep it clean and steady
Open the curtains wide and stand in the light
Say one true, kind thing to the first person you meet
Water a plant and wish it well
Say aloud: good thoughts, good words, good deeds
Tidy the place where you keep your light

rules.why: Catch a mean, envious or despairing thought today and replace it on purpose with a better one.
Tell no lies, break no promises and speak ill of no one. Say one thing that encourages.
Do at least one useful thing for someone else or for the world, and do it today.

rules.text: Keep water, earth and fire clean
rules.why: No litter, nothing foul down the drain, no waste. Leave the elements as you would want to find them.
Sadness nursed is a kind of defeat. Take pleasure in food, company and work, and bring some to others.
Wealth is good when it is earned honestly and shared. Part of what you have goes to those who lack.

read.title: The Hymns of Zoroaster
read.creator: trans. M. L. West
read.why: The seventeen Gathas in clear English with a long introduction. The prophet’s own voice, so far as it can be recovered.

read.title: Zoroastrians: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices
read.creator: Mary Boyce
read.why: The classic one-volume history by the scholar who lived among the villagers of Yazd.

read.title: Zoroastrianism: An Introduction
read.creator: Jenny Rose
read.why: An up-to-date and even-handed guide, from the Gathas to the diaspora.

read.title: Shahnameh: The Persian Book of Kings
read.creator: Abolqasem Ferdowsi, trans. Dick Davis
read.why: The national epic of Iran, written by a Muslim poet from Zoroastrian sources. Zarathustra, the sacred fires and the old kings are all in it.

read.title: Such a Long Journey
read.creator: Rohinton Mistry
read.why: A Parsi bank clerk in Bombay in 1971. The prayers, the tower of silence and the daily worries of a small community, in a fine novel.

read.title: The Crow Eaters
read.creator: Bapsi Sidhwa
read.why: A comic novel of a Parsi family making its fortune in Lahore a century ago.

watch.title: Little Zizou
watch.creator: Sooni Taraporevala
watch.why: A sweet comedy about two feuding Parsi families in Mumbai, one headed by a fanatic and the other by a liberal newspaperman.

watch.title: On Wings of Fire
watch.creator: Cyrus Bharucha
watch.why: A documentary history of the religion presented by the conductor Zubin Mehta, himself a Parsi.

watch.title: Qissa-e Parsi: The Parsi Story
watch.creator: Divya Cowasji and Shilpi Gulati
watch.why: A short documentary on the community’s history, humour and anxieties about its shrinking numbers.

watch.title: Pestonjee
watch.creator: Vijaya Mehta
watch.why: A quiet drama of friendship, envy and marriage among Bombay Parsis in the 1950s.

listen.title: Avestan prayers: Ashem Vohu and Yatha Ahu Vairyo
listen.creator: Recited by Zoroastrian priests; many recordings
listen.why: The two short prayers every Zoroastrian knows. The second is said to be the oldest of all.

listen.title: Also sprach Zarathustra
listen.creator: Richard Strauss
listen.why: A tone poem after Nietzsche, whose Zarathustra is his own invention. The opening sunrise is the most famous use of the prophet’s name in the West.

listen.title: Die Zauberflöte
listen.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
listen.why: The wise priest of the sun in The Magic Flute is called Sarastro, an Italian form of Zoroaster.

listen.title: Bohemian Rhapsody
listen.creator: Queen
listen.why: Freddie Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara to a Parsi family in Zanzibar and had a Zoroastrian funeral.

art.title: The winged figure at Persepolis
art.creator: Achaemenid stone carvers, Fars, Iran
art.why: A bearded man in a winged ring hovers over the king in the doorways of the palace. Scholars debate whether he is Ahura Mazda, the royal glory or a guardian spirit.

art.title: The investiture of Ardashir I
art.creator: Naqsh-e Rustam, Fars, Iran
art.why: A rock relief in which the god Ohrmazd, on horseback, hands the ring of kingship to the first Sasanian king. Each horse tramples an enemy, and the god’s is Ahriman.

art.title: The Cube of Zoroaster
art.creator: Naqsh-e Rustam, Fars, Iran
art.why: A square stone tower facing the royal tombs. Its purpose is unknown, and the name is medieval.

art.title: Sasanian silver plates
art.creator: Royal workshops of Iran
art.why: Gilded dishes showing kings hunting lions and boar: an image of the good ruler overcoming disorder. Fine examples are in St Petersburg, London and New York.

eat.title: Dhansak
eat.creator: Lentils, vegetables and meat cooked together, with caramelised brown rice
eat.why: The best known Parsi dish, mixing Persian and Gujarati cooking. It is eaten on Sundays and never at celebrations.

eat.title: Ash-e reshteh
eat.creator: Thick soup of herbs, beans and noodles
eat.why: Eaten in Iran at the new year. The noodles stand for the paths of the year ahead.

eat.title: Ravo
eat.creator: Sweet semolina pudding with rosewater, nuts and raisins
eat.why: Made on birthdays and auspicious mornings in Parsi homes.

eat.title: Sabzi polo ba mahi
eat.creator: Herbed rice with fish
eat.why: The meal for the first day of Nowruz across Iran.

drink.title: Parsi choi
drink.creator: Black tea brewed with mint and lemongrass
drink.why: The morning tea of Parsi households.

drink.title: Falooda
drink.creator: Cold milk with rose syrup, basil seeds and vermicelli
drink.why: Drunk at the new year. The Persian original is a frozen noodle sherbet from Shiraz.

drink.title: Pomegranate juice
drink.creator: Fresh pressed
drink.why: The pomegranate is a tree of plenty and immortality in Iranian tradition, and its twigs are used in ritual.

customs.title: Praying toward light
customs.creator: Sun, fire or lamp
customs.why: A Zoroastrian turns to a source of light to pray. In a fire temple worshippers bring sandalwood and take a pinch of ash for the forehead.

customs.title: The haft-sin table
customs.creator: Seven things beginning with the letter s
customs.why: For Nowruz families lay out sprouted wheat, garlic, apple, vinegar, sumac, dried oleaster and wheat pudding, with a mirror, candles and a book of wisdom.

customs.title: Chalk at the threshold
customs.creator: Chowk
customs.why: Parsi doorsteps are stamped each morning with patterns in white chalk powder, and doorways are hung with garlands.

customs.title: Sugar in the milk
customs.creator: A founding story
customs.why: When Persian refugees landed in Gujarat, the local king sent a full bowl of milk to say there was no room. Their priest stirred in sugar and sent it back: we will sweeten without spilling.

games.title: Backgammon (nard)
games.creator: Board game · Persia
games.why: A Middle Persian text says the sage Bozorgmehr invented it as an image of fate: the board is the earth, the dice are the turning heavens, and the player still has to choose.

games.title: Chess (chatrang)
games.creator: Board game · India and Sasanian Persia
games.why: The same text tells how chess came from India to the court of Khosrow I. The words check and mate come from the Persian for the king is helpless.

games.title: Prince of Persia
games.creator: Video game · Ubisoft Montreal
games.why: A wanderer and a princess heal a land corrupted by the dark god Ahriman, who has broken out of the tree where the god of light, Ormazd, imprisoned him. A loose but direct use of the myth.

festivals.title: Nowruz
festivals.creator: 20 or 21 March
festivals.why: The new year at the spring equinox. Houses are cleaned, the haft-sin table is laid and thirteen days of visiting follow. Many Parsis also keep a new year in August, by an older calendar.

festivals.title: Sadeh
festivals.creator: 30 January
festivals.why: A midwinter festival of fire, fifty days before the new year. A great bonfire is lit at dusk.

festivals.title: Mehregan
festivals.creator: Early October
festivals.why: The autumn festival of Mithra, guardian of contracts and friendship.

festivals.title: The six Gahambars
festivals.creator: Spread through the year
festivals.why: Seasonal feasts of five days each, marked by communal meals to which everyone contributes and at which everyone sits together.

places.title: Yazd
places.creator: Central Iran
places.why: The desert city where the faith held on. The fire in its temple is said to have burned since about 470 CE and can be seen through glass. The towers of silence stand on hills outside. Check current travel advice for Iran.

places.title: Chak Chak (Pir-e Sabz)
places.creator: Yazd Province, Iran
places.why: A shrine in a cliff where water drips from the rock. Thousands of Zoroastrians make a pilgrimage here each June.

places.title: Persepolis and Naqsh-e Rustam
places.creator: Fars Province, Iran
places.why: The ceremonial capital of Darius and the rock tombs of the Achaemenid kings, with Sasanian reliefs below them.

places.title: Udvada
places.creator: Gujarat, India
places.why: A quiet seaside town that houses the Iranshah, the holiest Parsi fire, burning since the refugees first consecrated it. In India only Zoroastrians may enter fire temples. The town and its museum are open to all.

places.title: Takht-e Soleyman
places.creator: West Azerbaijan Province, Iran
places.why: The ruins of a great Sasanian fire temple round a crater lake, where kings came on foot after their coronation.

ethics.title: Truth above all
ethics.text: To lie is to join the wrong side of the cosmic struggle. Keeping one’s word, especially in contracts and debts, is a religious duty.
ethics.practice: Make one promise today and keep it to the minute.

ethics.title: Active goodness
ethics.text: Avoiding evil is only the beginning. A person must do good, build, plant, heal and earn. The religion distrusts fasting, celibacy and withdrawal.
ethics.practice: Add one good thing to the world today that was not there this morning.

ethics.title: Charity
ethics.text: Wealth honestly made is praised, and so is giving it away. Parsi families endowed hospitals, schools and housing open to all communities.
ethics.practice: Give to something that helps people you will never meet.

ethics.title: Care for creation
ethics.text: Water, earth, fire, plants and animals are sacred trusts. Polluting them is a sin and tending them is worship.
ethics.practice: Clean up one place you did not dirty.

ethics.title: Responsibility
ethics.text: Every person chooses freely between truth and the lie, and answers for the choice. No one can be saved by another’s merit.
ethics.practice: Own one mistake today without explaining it away.

ethics.title: Joy
ethics.text: Happiness is a virtue and a weapon against evil. Festivals, feasting, marriage and laughter are commanded.
ethics.practice: Organise a small pleasure for other people this week.

philosophy.title: The two spirits
philosophy.text: In the beginning, says Zarathustra, there were twin spirits, the better and the bad in thought, word and deed, and between them the wise chose rightly. Good and evil are choices before they are forces.
philosophy.practice: Notice one fork in the road today, however small, and take the better branch on purpose.

philosophy.title: Free will
philosophy.text: Human beings are made free. The Wise Lord does not compel, and the world’s outcome depends in part on what people decide. This may be the oldest clear statement of moral freedom.
philosophy.practice: Catch yourself saying I had no choice. Check whether it is true.

philosophy.title: A good world, under attack
philosophy.text: The material world is the good creation of a good God. Death, decay and cruelty are an invasion and do not belong to the design. So the body, food, work and family are to be enjoyed and defended.
philosophy.practice: Take full pleasure in one good physical thing today and give thanks for it.

philosophy.title: Partners in the repair
philosophy.text: People are fellow workers with God in driving evil out of the world. Every true word and useful act shortens the struggle. The end, the making wonderful, is certain, and each person has a hand in it.
philosophy.practice: Pick one small wrong within your reach and put it right.

philosophy.title: Asha
philosophy.text: The same word names the order of nature and the rightness of an act. To be truthful is to move with the grain of the universe.
philosophy.practice: Find one thing in your life that is out of true: a misaligned habit or a crooked arrangement. Straighten it.

philosophy.title: Thought first
philosophy.text: Good thoughts come first in the formula because words and deeds grow from them. Guarding the mind is the first discipline.
philosophy.practice: Follow one resentful thought back to its start. Decide what you will think instead.

philosophy.title: Conscience as a mirror
philosophy.text: At the bridge the soul meets its own conscience in the shape of a woman, lovely or foul, who says: I was beautiful and you made me more beautiful, or the reverse. Judgment is self-recognition.
philosophy.practice: Ask what your conduct this week would look like if it had a face.

philosophy.title: Wisdom
philosophy.text: The supreme being is named Wisdom. Zarathustra asks questions, tells his hearers to reflect with a clear mind and to choose for themselves. Blind faith is not asked for.
philosophy.practice: Take one thing you believe on someone’s say-so and look into it yourself.

intro: Zoroastrianism is the religion taught by the prophet Zarathustra, whom the Greeks called Zoroaster. It may be the oldest of the world’s revealed religions, and it was for a thousand years the faith of the largest empires on earth. Today it has perhaps 120,000 followers, most of them in India, where they are known as Parsis, and in Iran. Few religions so small have given so much to others.

No one knows exactly when or where Zarathustra lived. The language of his hymns points to the eastern Iranian world, somewhere between the Aral Sea and Afghanistan, and to a date that scholars put anywhere from about 1500 to 600 BCE. He was a priest among cattle-herding people. In a vision by a river he came to see that there is one God, Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord, wholly good, and that the world is the scene of a struggle between truth and the lie in which every person must choose a side.

That choice is made in thought, word and deed. The world is good, made by a good God, and has been invaded by a hostile spirit that brings death and falsehood. Human beings are free and are needed. By thinking clearly, speaking truly and acting well they help to drive evil back, and at the end of time the world will be made wonderful, the dead raised and evil destroyed. Ideas of heaven and hell, a final judgment, a saviour to come and the resurrection appear here very early, and many scholars think they passed from Persia into Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

Worship centres on fire, the cleanest of the elements and the sign of truth. In the great temples a consecrated flame is fed five times a day and never allowed to go out. Believers wear a white shirt and a woven cord that they untie and retie with prayers, facing the light. The religion asks for an active, cheerful, useful life: marry, plant trees, earn honestly, give generously, keep the earth and water clean. It has no monks and does not prize fasting.

Under the Achaemenid kings Cyrus and Darius, the Parthians and then the Sasanians it was the religion of Iran. After the Arab conquest in the seventh century most Iranians gradually became Muslim. Some believers held on in the desert towns of Yazd and Kerman. Others sailed to Gujarat in western India, where their descendants, the Parsis, became shipbuilders, industrialists and philanthropists out of all proportion to their numbers.

This Onda borrows the shape of a Zoroastrian day: a morning renewal of the three commitments, time before a flame, one deliberately true word, an act of care for the physical world and an evening account. You are a guest. The sacred shirt and cord, the prayers in Avestan and the fire temple belong to those born or initiated into the faith.
guide.origin: The Iranian plateau and Central Asia; today Iran, India and a worldwide diaspora
guide.era: Zarathustra lived perhaps around 1200 BCE, perhaps as late as the 6th century BCE. His religion was the faith of three Persian empires

figures.name: Zarathustra
figures.bio: Priest, poet and prophet. Tradition says he received his vision at thirty, preached for ten years with one convert, and was at last accepted by King Vishtaspa.

figures.name: Vishtaspa
figures.bio: The ruler who became the prophet’s patron and protected the new teaching. His court is where the religion first took root.

figures.name: Cyrus the Great
figures.bio: Founder of the Persian empire, who let the peoples he conquered keep their gods and sent the Jewish exiles home. How far he was a Zoroastrian is debated.

figures.name: Darius I
figures.bio: He declares in his inscriptions that he is king by the favour of Ahuramazda and that his enemies followed the Lie.

figures.name: Kartir
figures.bio: A powerful Sasanian high priest who organised the state church, founded fires across the empire and persecuted other religions. His own inscriptions record it.

figures.name: Adurbad Mahraspandan
figures.bio: A high priest under Shapur II, remembered for his wise sayings and for proving the faith by an ordeal of molten metal.

figures.name: Jamsetji Tata
figures.bio: A Parsi industrialist of Bombay who founded what became India’s largest business group and gave much of his fortune to science and education.

figures.name: Dadabhai Naoroji
figures.bio: A Parsi scholar and politician, the first Indian elected to the British Parliament, who showed with figures how colonial rule drained India’s wealth.

figures.name: Mary Boyce
figures.bio: A British scholar who spent a year in a village near Yazd in the 1960s and transformed the modern study of the religion.

history.detail: He composes the Gathas in an eastern Iranian language. They are memorised by priests and passed on orally for well over a thousand years.
From Cyrus to Darius III the Persian kings rule from Egypt to India. Their inscriptions invoke Ahuramazda, and Greek writers describe the magi and their fires.
He allows deported peoples to go home. The Hebrew Bible calls him the Lord’s anointed. Jewish and Persian ideas are in contact for the next two centuries.
He burns Persepolis. Zoroastrian tradition remembers him as the accursed, who killed priests and scattered the scriptures.
A looser Iranian empire under which the religion continues and, by tradition, the first effort is made to collect the scattered texts.
Zoroastrianism becomes a state church with a hierarchy of priests. The Avesta is written down in a specially invented alphabet.
The last Sasanian king is killed in 651. Zoroastrians become a tolerated and taxed minority, and conversion to Islam proceeds over several centuries.
A group of believers from Khorasan sails to Gujarat. The Story of Sanjan, written in 1599, tells how a local king gave them leave to settle and they consecrated a fire.
Priests in Iran write down the great compilations of doctrine and myth, such as the Bundahishn and the Denkard, to save what could be saved.
Parsis move to the new British port and prosper as shipbuilders, traders and mill owners. They found schools, hospitals and the first Indian cricket club.
After long campaigning by Parsi envoys, the poll tax on Iran’s Zoroastrians is abolished. Their legal position slowly improves.
Communities form in Britain, North America and Australia. Numbers fall through low birth rates and marriage outside the faith, and the question of accepting converts is fiercely argued.

concepts.detail: The one eternal God, entirely good. He is not the source of evil and is not yet all-powerful over it, which is how the religion answers the problem of suffering.
Asha is cosmic and moral order. Druj is its denial. The righteous person is ashavan, a possessor of truth.

concepts.text: The origin of good and evil.
concepts.detail: The bounteous spirit and the hostile spirit chose life and not-life at the beginning. Later theology set Ohrmazd directly against Ahriman, giving the religion its dualist reputation.

concepts.text: Sky, water, earth, plants, animals, humankind, fire.
concepts.detail: Each was made perfect and each is protected by one of the bounteous immortals. The seven are honoured at the seasonal feasts.

concepts.text: The dignity of the human being.
concepts.detail: Each person chooses, and the choice matters to the fate of the world. Men and women are equally responsible.
Fires are graded in three ranks and tended by priests. Worshippers stand before the fire to pray to God. They do not pray to the fire.
Decay belongs to the hostile spirit, so earth, water and fire must not be polluted. Hence the old custom of exposing the dead on raised towers and not burying or burning them.
On the fourth dawn after death the soul is judged and crosses to the house of song or falls. Punishment is not eternal.
At the end a saviour born of the prophet’s line will raise the dead, all will pass through a river of molten metal that feels like warm milk to the righteous, and the world will be restored.

facts.text: The word magic comes from the magi, the Zoroastrian priests. The wise men who follow a star in the Gospel of Matthew are called magi.
The word paradise comes from an old Iranian word for a walled garden.
The Mazda car company chose its name partly for Ahura Mazda, as a symbol of wisdom and light.
The Iranshah fire at Udvada has, by tradition, burned without a break for more than a thousand years.

Traditional funerals expose the body to the sun and to vultures on a tower of silence. In Mumbai the collapse of the vulture population since the 1990s has forced the community to add solar concentrators.
Only about a quarter of the original Avesta is thought to survive. The rest was lost in the centuries after Alexander and the Arab conquest.

sensitivity.note: Zoroastrianism is a small, living religion that has survived centuries of pressure. This Onda borrows its ethic and the outline of its day. It does not reproduce the sacred cord, the Avestan prayers or temple worship, which belong to the community.
requiredCaveats: Most Parsi authorities do not accept converts, and non-Zoroastrians may not enter fire temples in India. Respect both.
Zoroastrians pray before fire as a symbol. Calling them fire worshippers is an old insult.
The dates and homeland of Zarathustra are uncertain, and scholars disagree about how much later religions took from his.
Iranian and Parsi practice differ, and so do reformist and traditional views within each.
